result:
The proposed answer is wrong. The method (minimum feedback arc set of the de Bruijn graph, with the block ordering assumed optimal) is reasonable, but the block ordering is not optimal, and the claimed optimality argument is only heuristic.

**Counterexample for k = 3.** The proposed formula gives n = 3(9−3+2)/2 = 12. But the following 11 triples work:

S = {111, 222, 333, 211, 212, 311, 312, 313, 321, 322, 323}

Take the vertex order (pairs (a,b) as graph vertices):

11 < 12 < 22 < 21 < 13 < 23 < 33 < 31 < 32

Every window abc is an edge (a,b)→(b,c). Removing S leaves the 16 windows 112, 113, 121, 122, 123, 131, 132, 133, 213, 221, 223, 231, 232, 233, 331, 332. Each goes forward in this order, so the remaining graph is acyclic. An infinite sequence over {1,2,3} would give an infinite walk, which a finite DAG cannot contain. So every infinite sequence contains a triple from S, and n ≤ 11 for k = 3.

The block ordering gives 12 for k = 3, so it is not optimal. The packing argument (eight arc-disjoint cycles plus three loops) shows n ≥ 11 for k = 3, so the true value there is 11. The formula n = k(k²−k+2)/2 therefore fails, and the value 495100 for k = 100 cannot be trusted.

(The formula does match k = 1 and k = 2, which is why the small cases looked convincing.)

VERDICT: REJECT
CONFIDENCE: 5
